title: Devices: enrollment, identity, topology and health
summary: A device in this farm is identified by where it is plugged in, not by what it calls itself: OEM serials collide, and this rack has a clone pair (0123456789ABCDEF at usb:3-1.1 and usb:3-1.2) to prove it. Identity is observed, then resolved against a four-rung ladder — branded uid, hardware fingerprint, serial-plus-slot, adopt — and then branded back onto the phone so the strongest rung exists next time. Health is a third clock kept strictly apart from leases: the watchdog writes one table, has no privilege on farm.leases at all, and a device going offline never takes it away from a running job. Read the Gaps before you rely on any of the enrollment or topology machinery: on PostgreSQL 17 the fingerprint rung cannot execute, and neither enrollment nor topology discovery runs anywhere except the farmd node role on Linux.

sections.heading: The rule everything on this page obeys
sections.body:
A lease ends when the job says so, when a deadline the user wrote down elapses, or when a human takes it back. Nothing on this page can end one. That is enforced three ways.

**By imports.** `internal/adbwire`, `internal/enroll`, `internal/topo` and `internal/watchdog` do not import `internal/lease` — verified by grep across all four packages. There is no function in scope in any of them that could end, shorten or even read a lease. A change that needs a lease value in one of them is proof the change belongs elsewhere.

**By grants.** `migrations/00002_lease.sql:80` does `REVOKE ALL ON farm.leases FROM farm_watchdog`. Checked against the running server below. (What that revoke is worth at runtime is a gap — see Gaps.)

**By vocabulary.** `farm.leases.release_reason` has a CHECK constraint listing seven values — `completed`, `failed`, `job_cancelled`, `max_runtime`, `operator_revoked`, `holder_expired`, `device_retired` (`migrations/00001_core.sql:324`). None of them is a connectivity value, so "the socket broke" raises check_violation rather than silently destroying work. That is the direct answer to DeviceFarmer/STF issue #663, where a ~90-minute ECONNRESET on the tracking socket released a device mid-run.

The cost of the rule is stated plainly in `internal/adbwire/doc.go`: when the tracker's connection drops, **no snapshot is emitted at all**. The package does not synthesise an empty device list and does not mark anything absent. Losing the socket to an ADB server is evidence about the socket, not about the phones behind it.
bullets: A transport failure in `adbwire` has exactly two permitted effects: a typed error returned to the immediate caller, and a counter incremented (`internal/adbwire/doc.go:22-27`).
`topo` marks a slot `maintenance` when its port leaves the USB tree; it cannot end the lease of a device sitting in that slot (`internal/topo/discover.go:28-32`).
`enroll` refuses to clear another device row's slot pointer to make room for a newcomer — that row may be holding a live lease this second (`internal/enroll/enroll.go:772-781`).

The watchdog's `healthFor` maps `offline` to health `offline` (`internal/watchdog/watchdog.go:876-877`). That is a statement about the wire, and the function's own comment says it may never be read as a reason to take a device away.

sections.heading: An ADB serial is evidence, not an identifier
sections.body:
Cheap OEMs ship batches of handsets with the same burned-in serial. STF's own README documents a device shipping as `0123456789ABCDEF`, and this rack has two of them.

The consequence is not cosmetic. Every recovery action in this system — reconnect, detach/attach, USB reset, port power cycle, reboot — resolves a target before it acts. If it resolved by serial, it could land on the clone that is four hours into somebody's six-hour run and kill it, while the broken phone next to it stays broken. So **every addressed call in this codebase takes a devpath**, the position in the USB tree, and the serial is recorded as an observation and used only as one component of a digest.

Serial addressing exists in exactly one function, `adbwire.Client.UnsafeBySerial` (`client.go:407-419`), and carries that name deliberately. It has no callers in production code — only in `client_test.go`, where the test asserts that a clone serial comes back as `ErrAmbiguousTarget`. `doc.go:45-49` scopes it to interactive tooling and to bootstrap enrolment of a device whose devpath is not yet known, and forbids any recovery or health path from calling it.

The schema records the collision rather than hiding it. `farm.devices.serial_ambiguous` is set from inside `farm.resolve_device` in two places: rung 3 sets it the moment it sees more than one row carrying the serial (`00004_operate.sql:307`), and rung 4 re-checks *after* an adoption (`:352`), because at the moment the second clone is first resolved the count is still one and neither device would ever be flagged.
bullets: `farm.slots.adb_devpath` is `GENERATED ALWAYS AS ('usb:' || usb_path) STORED` (`migrations/00001_core.sql:100`) — the join key between the schema and what the ADB server reports.
`adbwire.Client.Devices` uses `host:devices-l` and never falls back to the short form, because the short form omits the devpath (`client.go:246-261`).

`adbwire.Snapshot.AmbiguousSerials()` sorts its result (`device.go:184-186`): the value ends up in operator logs, and an unstable order would make two identical observations look like two different ones.

A device the ADB server lists with no devpath — an emulator, a network target — cannot be addressed by position and `Device.Target()` refuses rather than falling back to the serial (`device.go:113-130`). It has no place in a rack and cannot be power-cycled.

examples.label: Find the clone pair
examples.code:
SELECT d.farm_uid, d.model, s.adb_devpath, s.rack_slot, d.serial_ambiguous
  FROM farm.devices d
  JOIN farm.slots s ON s.id = d.current_slot_id
 WHERE d.adb_serial IN (SELECT adb_serial FROM farm.devices
                         GROUP BY adb_serial HAVING count(*) > 1)
 ORDER BY s.adb_devpath;
examples.note: Two different handsets — a Pixel 7 and a Pixel 6a — reporting one serial. Separate rows, separate uids, separate rack positions. On this demo the flag was seeded, not observed; see Gaps.

examples.label: What serial addressing does instead
examples.code:
# host-serial:<target>:<cmd> — the target-name field, matched against
# serial OR devpath, exactly as adb's atransport::MatchesTarget does
SENT   : 0026host-serial:0123456789ABCDEF:get-state
examples.output:
STATUS : FAIL
LENGTH : 0014 (20 bytes)
PAYLOAD:
more than one device
examples.note: A refusal is the good outcome. The dangerous outcome is a server build that picks one, which is why nothing in the recovery or health paths is allowed to address by serial at all.

examples.label: What the devpath validator accepts
examples.output:
"usb:3-1.4.2"            true
"usb:3-1.1"              true
"usb:20-3"               true      <- Darwin location form
"usb:3-1.4:reboot"       false     <- a colon would terminate the service field early
"usb:3-1.4 usb:3-1.5"    false     <- a space would too
"usb:3-1.4\nhost:kill"   false     <- a newline
"0123456789ABCDEF"       false     <- a serial is not a position
"emulator-5554"          false
""                       false
examples.note: The pattern is a security boundary, not formatting hygiene. A devpath is interpolated into a colon-delimited service string, and the request on the other end of a retarget may be a reboot aimed at a phone three hours into somebody else's run. One predicate, `isDevpath`, backs both the listing parser and `ValidateDevpath`, so what this package will record and what it will address cannot drift apart.

sections.heading: The resolution ladder: brand → fingerprint → serial AND slot → adopt
sections.body:
The decision "which device is this?" lives in exactly one place: `farm.resolve_device`, `migrations/00004_operate.sql:245`. It is SQL rather than Go on purpose — a second copy of the ladder in Go would drift from the one in the database, and the two would disagree about which phone this is. `internal/enroll` carries evidence in and an answer out and nothing else (`enroll.go:720-753`).

The first thing the function does is look up the slot for `(host_id, usb_path)` and **RAISE `no_data_found` if there is none** (`:266-270`). Adoption needs a position; registering positions is topology's job, not enrollment's. `internal/enroll` therefore reads the slot list itself once per cycle (`enroll.go:466-489`) rather than letting that exception abort the transaction that was recording the sighting.

Then four rungs, strongest evidence first.
bullets: **Rung 1 — branded farm uid.** We wrote it, so it is ours. A device carrying a brand is always resolvable, whatever else it did or did not say (`identity.go:204-218`).

**Rung 2 — hardware fingerprint.** A digest over the properties a factory reset does not touch. If exactly one device matches, that is the device; more than one and the answer is `ambiguous` with no device named. **This rung raises SQLSTATE 42883 on PostgreSQL 17 — see Gaps. It is the first rung a brand-new phone reaches.**

**Rung 3 — serial AND the slot it was last seen in.** A serial on its own identifies nothing. Both must agree. If the serial is carried by more than one row, `serial_ambiguous` is set on every one of them and no device is named.

**Rung 4 — adopt.** Mint `df-` + 16 random bytes hex, insert into `farm.devices`, create the `farm.device_runtime` row (which defaults to health `unknown`), then re-check for a serial collision that only became visible after the insert.

Whichever rung answers, occupancy is recorded: any stale tenancy is closed (`device moved`, `slot reoccupied`) and the current one opened in `farm.slot_occupancy`, which carries unique partial indexes forcing one live device per slot and one live slot per device (`00004_operate.sql:90-92`).

examples.label: Rung 1 — the branded device (rolled back, nothing changed)
Rung 3 — a unique serial in the slot it was last seen in
Rung 3 on a CLONE serial — this is the case to understand
examples.note: The `ambiguous` verdict computed at rung 3 is DISCARDED: rung 4 tests only `IF v_dev IS NULL`, which is still true. A third row now carries that serial. Brand your devices; the fingerprint and serial rungs are the fallback, not the plan. Note the slot id: identity sequences are not transactional, so a rollback still consumes the number and your run will print a different one.

If it does fire — the slot vanished mid-cycle — classifyResolveError maps P0002 to the same outcome.

sections.heading: The hardware fingerprint: what it hashes and what it deliberately does not
sections.body:
The fingerprint's whole job is to recognise a phone that came back **wiped**. A factory reset erases `/data`, which is where the brand lives, where `Settings.Secure.android_id` lives, and where anything an app could have written lives. So the digest is built only from read-only partition and bootloader data.

Five components, in fixed order, each length-prefixed (`%d:%s`) so that `("ab","c")` and `("a","bc")` cannot hash alike:

`manufacturer` · `model` · `device` (board codename) · `hardware` (SoC/platform) · `serial` (first non-empty of `ro.boot.serialno`, `ro.serialno`, the ADB serial).

**The build properties are excluded on purpose.** `ro.build.fingerprint` and `ro.build.version.*` survive a factory reset too, but they do not survive an OTA. A fleet-wide update would change the fingerprint of every device on the same night: the ladder would fall through to serial-and-slot for the entire rack at once, and any phone that had also been re-cabled would be adopted as new. A wipe loses one device's brand; an OTA that reset every fingerprint would lose the fleet's.

**The serial is required, and at least three of the five components must be present** (`fingerprintMinComponents = 3`). Without a serial every unit of one model hashes identically and `resolve_device` reports `ambiguous` for the whole rack. Below three components the digest stops distinguishing units and starts grouping them, which is worse than no digest at all. Below the bar the function returns `nil`, which is not an error — resolution simply moves down the ladder.

The digest is prefixed with `device-farmer/hwfp/1`. When the component set is eventually revised, the version bump makes the new digests visibly different rather than quietly colliding with the old ones.

examples.label: Real HardwareFingerprint output
examples.output:
3-1.1 Pixel 7                        9866b639890cbf7fd32aa502053c2ae333da4db5a012d0079a5ae289994668f1  [manufacturer model device hardware serial]
3-1.2 Pixel 6a                       c6d5aa8e0e382da16699dbd0437b9cbaa0a6c0ef4b1a1447b21f1d81e50690e4  [manufacturer model device hardware serial]
model + serial only (2 components)   nil  (below the bar)
no serial at all                     nil  (below the bar)
two identical units, same serial     9866b639890cbf7fd32aa502053c2ae333da4db5a012d0079a5ae289994668f1  [manufacturer model device hardware serial]
examples.note: The clone pair fingerprints APART because the model and board differ — which is why a fingerprint is stronger evidence than a serial. The last line is the honest limit: two genuinely identical units carrying the same serial produce the same digest, `resolve_device` answers `ambiguous`, and no device is named. That is the correct answer, not a bug.

sections.heading: Branding: where the farm writes its own name on the device
sections.body:
The brand is the strongest rung because we wrote it. It lives at **`/data/local/tmp/.farm/uid`** — the one directory an ADB shell can write on a stock, non-rooted phone. It is inside `/data`, so a factory reset erases it, which is precisely the case the hardware fingerprint exists to cover.

The uid is minted by `farm.resolve_device` (`'df-' || encode(gen_random_bytes(16),'hex')`) and read back out of `farm.devices.farm_uid` before it is written to the phone. `internal/enroll` never invents one: a uid this process made up would name a row that does not exist. The format is a CHECK constraint on `farm.devices.farm_uid` (`^df-[0-9a-f]{32}$`, `00001_core.sql:135`) and the same regex in Go (`brand.go:38`) — checked before the value is put into a shell command, which also happens to make it shell-inert.

Branding is idempotent and **never overwrites a different uid**. Two farm uids on one device means two rows in `farm.devices` believe they are this phone; overwriting one would merge two devices' histories — failure scores, quarantines, lease records — into a single row with no way afterwards to tell which measurement belonged to which handset. That is refused, logged at ERROR, and written to `farm.events` as `identity_conflict`.
bullets: The write is atomic: `uid.new` then `mv -f`. A phone that loses power halfway must end up with the old brand or the new one, never half a uid — a truncated brand matches nothing and sends a known phone back down the ladder.
It is `sync`'d, with fallbacks, because the brand's whole purpose is to survive the abrupt reboots a recovery ladder causes.

The write **re-checks on the device** what the caller checked one round trip ago and refuses there with exit 17. Without that line, the one promise this package makes would rest on a `cat` having succeeded a second earlier.
The write is verified by reading the file back over a fresh connection. A write nobody read back is a write we only believe happened, and an unbranded device we think is branded gets adopted twice.

A brand file whose content is not a farm uid is recorded as `malformed_uid` in the observation detail and **never acted on** (`enroll.go:574`): something other than this system wrote that file, and the device will not be branded while it is there.

An empty brand file reads as unbranded on purpose, so a write that lost power can be replaced instead of blocking that device forever. Exit 44 means "there is no file", which is deliberately distinct from "the file could not be read" — `cat 2>/dev/null` gives both the same answer.

examples.label: The three commands, exactly as the code builds them
examples.code:
# Printed by running the real probeCommand, brandReadCmd and brandWriteCmd
# under `go test -overlay` (no file was added to the repository).

# PROBE — brand and eleven properties in ONE round trip. The brand is read
# first and printed first because it is the strongest evidence we will have.
printf '%s=%s\n' farm_uid "$(cat /data/local/tmp/.farm/uid 2>/dev/null)"; for k in ro.product.manufacturer ro.product.model ro.product.name ro.product.device ro.build.version.release ro.build.version.sdk ro.product.cpu.abilist ro.build.fingerprint ro.hardware ro.boot.serialno ro.serialno; do printf '%s=%s\n' "$k" "$(getprop "$k")"; done

# BRAND READ — exit 44 means "there is no file".
if [ -e /data/local/tmp/.farm/uid ]; then cat /data/local/tmp/.farm/uid; else exit 44; fi

# BRAND WRITE — exit 17 means the device found a different brand in place.
if [ -s /data/local/tmp/.farm/uid ] && [ "$(cat /data/local/tmp/.farm/uid 2>/dev/null)" != 'df-970e1c5b7163543ded6ed5f3a05c0978' ]; then exit 17; fi; mkdir -p /data/local/tmp/.farm && printf '%s' 'df-970e1c5b7163543ded6ed5f3a05c0978' > /data/local/tmp/.farm/uid.new && chmod 600 /data/local/tmp/.farm/uid.new && mv -f /data/local/tmp/.farm/uid.new /data/local/tmp/.farm/uid && { sync /data/local/tmp/.farm/uid 2>/dev/null || sync 2>/dev/null || true; }
examples.output: (the three strings above are the verbatim output)
examples.note: One round trip rather than twelve is not micro-optimisation: a host probes every attached device on every cycle, each ADB call is a fresh connect and transport negotiation, and some of those devices are mid-job.

sections.heading: Observe before you conclude: farm.identity_observations
sections.body:
Every cycle inserts the sighting **first, in its own statement**, before `farm.resolve_device` is called (`enroll.go:606` calls `observe`, `:620` calls `resolve`). That ordering is the whole reason the table exists: a failure in resolution — an unknown position, a slot whose previous occupant is still recorded in it, a database that rejects the call — still leaves behind a durable record of what was physically seen. Weeks later, that record is the only thing that can explain why a device was adopted, or why it was not.

The row carries what the ADB server said (`usb_path`, `adb_devpath`, `transport_id`, `adb_serial`), what the device said about itself (`farm_uid`, `hw_fingerprint`, `manufacturer`, `model`, `product`, `device_codename`, `android_release`, `sdk_int`, `abis`, `build_fingerprint`), the `host_epoch` the transport id was minted in, and a `resolution` that starts at `pending`. `observed_at` is the column default `now()` — the INSERT never passes a timestamp, so no reading from the enrolling process's clock is ever written.

The conclusion is attached afterwards with `detail = detail || $jsonb` (`enroll.go:821-825`). The merge matters: the observation's own evidence must survive the conclusion.
bullets: `resolution` CHECK: `pending`, `branded_uid`, `hw_fingerprint`, `serial_and_slot`, `adopted_new`, `ambiguous`, `conflict`, `unreadable` (`00004_operate.sql:45-48`).
`unreadable` covers a device that answered nothing usable: `unauthorized`, `offline`, `probe_timeout`, `probe_truncated`, `probe_noisy`, `detached`, `probe_failed`, `identity_incomplete`.

`cancelled` is deliberately NOT recorded (`enroll.go:545-547`). A probe this process abandoned on the way out is a fact about a shutdown; putting it in the record would enter a deployment into evidence against a phone.
A partial or over-long probe answer is recorded but never resolved on. Half a property list is indistinguishable from a different device's property list, and adoption on it mints a phantom.

Every device-supplied string is bounded and made storable before it goes near the database (`identity.go:56-75`): PostgreSQL rejects a NUL byte and invalid UTF-8 (22021 on text, 22P05 on jsonb), and one bad byte would fail the whole INSERT — losing the *sighting*, on every cycle, forever, with nothing saying why.

Only two outcomes get a `farm.events` row: `device_adopted` (`enroll.go:656`) and `identity_conflict` (`:930`). A cycle that recognises forty known devices writes forty observation rows and no events, because a timeline at one line per device per cycle is a timeline nobody reads.
`ident_obs_conflict` is a partial index on `(observed_at DESC) WHERE resolution IN ('ambiguous','conflict','unreadable')` — the query an operator actually runs.

examples.label: What went wrong, most recent first
examples.code:
SELECT observed_at, host_id, usb_path, resolution,
       detail->>'reason'     AS reason,
       detail->>'unreadable' AS unreadable,
       adb_serial
  FROM farm.identity_observations

sections.heading: How USB topology becomes slots, hubs, controllers and power domains
sections.body:
A **slot is a position**: bus, hub, port. It is what a human can walk to, what a power switch can cut, and what survives the device in it being unplugged, replaced, reflashed or renamed. Devices come and go from slots.

Discovery reads the Linux USB tree from `/sys/bus/usb/devices` through an `fs.FS`, which is why the parser and the label arithmetic are testable on any machine while the real source refuses to run anywhere but Linux. `topo.Sysfs` fails explicitly off Linux rather than returning an empty tree, because **an empty tree is the dangerous answer**: discovery would conclude that every slot on the host has vanished.

Two sysfs details drive the parsing and are easy to get wrong. The entries under `/sys/bus/usb/devices` are symlinks into `/sys/devices`, so nothing here filters on `IsDir` and nothing uses `fs.WalkDir` (which does not follow symlinks and would see an empty tree on a real host). And a root hub's directory is named `usb3` while it addresses itself as `3-0`, with a device in its first root port being `3-1`, not `3-0.1`.

What becomes a slot is deliberately conservative. A hub joins the farm when it is carrying at least one Android device — recognised by the USB interface triple `ff/42/01` (ADB) or `ff/42/03` (fastboot), which is what adb's own host code matches on and does not depend on a vendor-id table. A hub full of dongles on somebody's desk does not become fourteen slots because it happens to share a machine.
bullets: Every port of an adopted hub becomes a slot, occupied or not: the empty socket next to seven full ones is where the eighth phone goes, and the slot has to exist before the device does.
A port carrying another hub is skipped. Registering it would create a slot whose `usb_path` is a hub's `usb_path`, and a recovery action aimed at that "device" would be aimed at a hub.

Root hubs are excluded by default. Even with `IncludeRootHubs`, only ports currently holding an Android device become slots — a root hub's other ports are the machine's own keyboard, NIC and BMC, and turning those into schedulable positions is how an operator power-cycles the host's boot drive to recover a phone.
Hubs below `MinPorts` (default `DefaultMinHubPorts = 3`) are ignored: the two-port hub inside a monitor, the one inside a keyboard.

Registration is per hub, each in its own transaction (`registerHub`, `discover.go:637-682`). A hub is the natural unit — its controller, its power domain and its ports are one consistent statement about one piece of hardware — so a failure part-way leaves whole hubs registered rather than half a hub.

`registerHub` returns a non-zero count only after `tx.Commit` succeeds. Reporting rolled-back rows as written puts a number in the report and in `farm_topo_slots_registered_total` that nothing in the database backs, which is how an operator concludes a rack was registered and stops looking.

`linkHubs` sets `farm.hubs.parent_hub_id` afterwards, because `register_slot` handles one hub at a time and cannot know the upstream one exists yet. Blast-radius correlation reads that tree: a five-port hub daisy-chained off another fails as a unit with its parent.

sections.heading: Why a hub without per-port switching gets ONE ganged domain
sections.body:
`farm.power_domains` models **what a single switch actually controls**. On a hub without per-port VBUS switching, every port shares one domain, so "power-cycle this device" is really "power-cycle these seven devices" — six of which may be mid-run, holding live leases.

`farm.register_slot` therefore creates exactly one domain per hub path and sets its kind from the hub's switching capability: `per_port`/`uhubctl` when the hardware proves it can switch one port, `ganged`/`none` otherwise (`00004_operate.sql:411-423`). The comment in the migration is blunt about why this lives in SQL rather than Go: it is what stops the recovery ladder from power-cycling seven devices to fix one.

**Positive evidence is required to claim per-port; the absence of evidence is never read as capability.** `hubPower` in `sysfs.go` reads `wHubCharacteristics` bits 1..0 (00 ganged, 01 individual, 1x none) when the kernel exposes it, and otherwise counts per-port `disable` attributes — requiring the attribute to be present *and writable* on **every** port (`writableAttr`, `sysfs.go:484-490`), because a read-only `disable` is a status readout, not a control. Anything ambiguous — some ports controllable, some not, no attribute at all, an interface directory that would not list — resolves to `unknown`, which callers treat as not switchable.

Erring toward ganged costs a wider blast radius on a recovery attempt and a refusal. Erring the other way costs somebody's six-hour run.

`reconcilePower` exists because `register_slot` creates a domain on first sight and never revisits it — correct for a schema function, wrong for a rack where somebody swapped a switchable hub for a cheap one in the same socket. **The downgrade to `ganged` is the load-bearing direction.** The upgrade happens only on positive evidence, and both UPDATEs are restricted to the exact `('ganged','none')` / `('per_port','uhubctl')` shapes `register_slot` itself writes, so a domain an operator pointed at a PDU or a smart hub is left alone.

sections.heading: rack_slot: the string a human walks to at 03:00
sections.body:
A `rack_slot` is what an operator reads when a page says a device is unreachable. `R2-U14-H3-P5` sends them to a rack, a shelf, a hub and a socket. `30501029-78dd-4fd9` sends them to a spreadsheet, and then to the wrong device.

Four fields and nothing else: `R<rack>` from `farm.hosts.rack_id`, `U<unit>` from `farm.hosts.rack_unit` (zero-padded to two digits so labels sort the way shelves stack), `H<token>` for the hub, `P<port>` for the socket. A host with no rack coordinates falls back to its host id, because a label with no locus is unwalkable.

**The hub token is a pure function of the USB path**, not an enumeration ordinal. The obvious choice — "this is the third hub I found" — is wrong in a way that is invisible until it hurts. sysfs enumeration order reflects which hub answered first during boot, module load order, and what was already plugged in when the kernel came up; reboot the host and the third hub becomes the first. A sorted index is stable only while the set of hubs is unchanged; racking one more hub in an earlier root port renumbers everything after it.

And the failure is silently destructive. `farm.register_slot`'s conflict arm is `rack_slot = COALESCE(EXCLUDED.rack_slot, farm.slots.rack_slot)`, and discovery always passes a computed label — so a shifted ordinal does not produce one bad label, it **rewrites every label on the host in a single pass, while an operator is walking toward a rack holding a printout of the old ones.**

So `HubOrdinal("3-1.4")` is `3.1.4`: the bus number plus the chain of physical sockets the cable actually runs through. That string changes when, and only when, a human moves a cable — which is exactly when the label *should* change.
bullets: The one non-physical part of a USB path is the bus number, which the kernel assigns in controller registration order. A kernel upgrade or a module load-order change can move it. That is what `Overrides.HubTokens` is for — pin `"3-1.4" -> "3"` and get the classic `R2-U14-H3-P5`. (It has no config surface today; see Gaps.)
`Overrides.SlotLabels` bypasses the scheme entirely, for the rack where somebody already stuck numbers on every socket.

Three collision checks, all before anything is written: `NewLabeler` rejects two overrides claiming one token; `Labeler.Check` catches an override colliding with a *derived* token; `checkPlannedLabels` catches two finished slot labels being equal. `farm.slots` has no unique index on `rack_slot` — verified against the live catalog — so without these the second write simply succeeds and two sockets answer to one label.

Error messages are emitted from sorted maps, so a config with two bad entries always reports the same one first. An error message that changes between runs of the same config is one operators stop believing.

sections.heading: Slot lifecycle: marked, never deleted
sections.body:
**Nothing in `topo` removes a slot because a device stopped answering.** A phone that boots into fastboot, drops off the bus, or has USB debugging switched off is still in its socket, and its slot still exists. The only thing that retires a slot is the *port itself* no longer being reported by the kernel — the hub was unplugged or replaced.

Even then the slot is marked `maintenance`, never deleted. `farm.leases`, `farm.recovery_attempts`, `farm.quarantines` and `farm.slot_occupancy` all reference slots by id, and a slot id in a six-month-old lease row has to keep resolving to a position a human can be told about. `maintenance` is also exactly the right semantics: `farm.lease_acquire` requires `s.state = 'active'` in both its candidate pick and its re-check under the lock (`00002_lease.sql:243`, `:265`), so a retired slot stops being scheduled and does nothing else. **It cannot end the lease of a device sitting in one** — a hub being unplugged is not a reason to take a running job's device away.

Removal reconciliation is guarded three ways, and is off by default.
bullets: **Off by default.** `RetireVanished` is false, because the first thing a new deployment does is scan a host whose slots were seeded by hand, and the second thing it should not do is retire all of them.

**Never on a partial scan.** If any sysfs entry failed to read, or a device referenced a parent the scan did not report, the tree is `Partial` and reconciliation is skipped with the note: an absent port is not evidence that the port is gone.

**Bounded.** One pass may retire at most `MaxRetireFraction` (default 0.25) of a host's active slots. The bound is a statement about evidence, not about hardware: hubs fail one at a time, and a pass claiming a quarter of a host disappeared at once is far more likely a udev hiccup, a container that lost its `/sys` bind mount, or a scan against the wrong machine. Acting on it would make every device on that host unschedulable — a farm outage caused by a bad read. One vanished slot is always allowed through (`len(vanished) > 1` gates the check), because pulling a single dead hub out of a small host exceeds any fraction and that case is obviously benign.
A scan that finds **zero** live ports on a host that has active slots is refused outright. That is not a host that lost its hardware; it is a scan that did not work.

`restore` reactivates **only** slots whose most recent `farm.audit_log` row is discovery's own actor with action `slot.maintenance`. A human who put a slot into maintenance ("this port is flaky, leave it out until I replace the cable") has the last word, and a timer waking up and undoing their decision behind their back is precisely the class of automation this system refuses to contain.

Running discovery twice against unchanged hardware writes nothing the second time. That is a correctness property, not an optimisation: discovery runs on a timer, and an operator must be able to tell a real topology change from routine noise by looking at `farm.events`.

sections.heading: The device state machine
sections.body:
Two vocabularies, kept apart on purpose.

**`farm.device_runtime.adb_state`** is what the wire says, verbatim from the ADB server, normalised into a closed set. `adbwire.ParseConnState` is total over that set — including the three values the server never emits — so a value read back out of the column parses to itself. Omitting `absent` from the exact-match arm would silently rewrite it to `unknown` on the way back in, turning "we have never seen this device" into "we cannot tell", which are different alarms. The server does not restrict itself to single words either: a permissions problem arrives as a whole sentence ending in a bracketed URL, so parsing matches on prefixes and substrings.

**`farm.device_runtime.health`** is the verdict the allocator reads. `absent` is ours, not the server's: it means the device was not in a real listing at all.

The allocator's predicate is narrow and appears twice in `farm.lease_acquire` — once to pick a candidate (`00002_lease.sql:238-247`), once to re-check under the lock (`:257-266`), because `ORDER BY` materialises the sort before locking and the row we locked may no longer qualify: `admin_state = 'enabled'` AND `current_lease_id IS NULL` AND `adb_state = 'device'` AND `health = 'healthy'` AND `s.state = 'active'` AND `s.rearm_at <= now()`.

rows: the ADB server cannot talk to it — a statement about the wire, never a reason to reclaim
the RSA dialog is still on screen; the most common state in a fresh rack
a REAL snapshot arrived that did not contain it
alive and addressable, just not able to run a test — the operator response differs from offline: one is a cable, the other is a mode
udev rules on the host, not a fault of the device
the absence of history, not a history of instability
a human verdict. No probe overturns it.
an administrative fact. No probe overturns it.

bullets: A new device's runtime row is created at health `unknown`, never `healthy` — both by `farm.resolve_device` (which inserts without a health value, taking the column default) and by the watchdog's `ensure` (`watchdog.go:739-754`). `unknown` means precisely "nobody has looked yet"; starting at `healthy` would let the allocator hand out a device on the strength of an assumption.

`unknown` gets one exception in the damper (`watchdog.go:660`): one good look is enough to leave it, because hysteresis exists to damp oscillation and there is nothing there to oscillate against. The flap token is still charged.

`suppress_until` freezes health while an induced reset is in flight (`watchdog.go:653`). The transport is *expected* to drop, so a drop proves nothing. It is set by the recovery ladder (`ladder.go:1070`), which also flips health to `recovering` for the settle window.

The ladder will not climb again until `updated_at > suppress_until` (`ladder.go:516-517`) — waiting only for the window to lapse would spend the next rung on the frozen value. Requiring a write after the window is what makes the settle window actually settle something.
In the demo these rules are only half in force: a second reconciler writes the same table with different logic and no `suppress_until` check. See Gaps.

sections.heading: The flap damper, and why it is asymmetric
sections.body:
A USB device on a marginal cable can enumerate and drop every few seconds. Reflecting that faithfully produces a health column that oscillates healthy ↔ degraded, an allocator that hands the device out between blips, and an alert nobody can act on.

`farm.device_runtime.flap_credits` is a token bucket (schema default 10.0, cap `DefaultFlapCap = 10.0`, refill `DefaultFlapRefill = 1.0` tokens/minute), **refilled against the server's `now()` from `flap_updated_at` recorded on the row itself**. No clock on the watchdog pod is consulted and none is sent: a watchdog with a skewed clock must not be able to hand a device a bucket full of tokens it did not earn. The whole decision — refill, hysteresis, transition, the credit charge — is one statement.

The asymmetry is the mechanism:

**Going down is free**, but debounced by `consec_bad` (`DefaultMinBad = 2`). Safety first: a device that is failing must leave the schedulable set promptly, and never at the mercy of an empty bucket.

**Coming back up costs one token**, on top of a `consec_good` hysteresis (`DefaultMinGood = 3`, higher than MinBad on purpose — claiming healthy is a promise to the allocator). A device that keeps bouncing runs its bucket dry and then **stays out of the pool** until it has been quiet long enough to refill.

The expensive direction is the one that would put a bad device back in front of a tenant.

The loop is a reconciler, not an event handler. The ADB server only speaks when something changes, so a purely edge-triggered loop writes nothing for a quiet rack — and a row changed underneath it (the ladder marking a device `recovering`, an operator closing a quarantine) would never converge. Every `Resync` (`DefaultResync = 60s`) the last **real** observation is applied again. If nothing has ever been observed on a host, nothing is applied: inventing an empty listing is exactly the mistake `adbwire` refuses to make on a dropped socket.

examples.label: Devices the ADB server can reach right now that are still not schedulable
examples.code:
SELECT s.rack_slot, r.adb_state, r.health, r.consec_good,
       round(r.flap_credits,2) AS credits, r.ladder_tier,
       r.suppress_until IS NOT NULL AS suppressed
  FROM farm.device_runtime r JOIN farm.slots s ON s.id = r.slot_id
 WHERE r.adb_state = 'device' AND r.health <> 'healthy'
 ORDER BY s.rack_slot;

sections.heading: What the watchdog may and may not touch
sections.body:
**May write:** `farm.device_runtime` (its own table) and its row in `farm.component_heartbeat` via `farm.component_beat`.

**May read:** `farm.devices`, `farm.slots`, `farm.hosts` — enough to know which position a device sits in and what its rack label is.

**May not touch, at all:** `farm.leases`, `farm.jobs`, `farm.devices` (writes).

Three specific refusals worth knowing:

**It will not set `farm.devices.serial_ambiguous`.** It detects the collision (`AmbiguousSerials`) and logs a warning, but `farm.devices` is not its table, and widening the grant to set one boolean would put the health plane inside the identity table (`watchdog.go:516-528`). The flag is set by `farm.resolve_device` instead — which means that on a farm where enrollment is not running, nobody sets it.

**It will not bump `farm.hosts.host_epoch`.** It only *copies* the epoch it captured at worker start, alongside every `transport_id` it records. Bumping is the node agent's job. Because adb reuses small transport integers across a restart, `(host_epoch, transport_id)` is the only stable pair (`00001_core.sql:40-43`) — and a worker still stamping the previous epoch is recording a pair that names a transport nobody has. That is why a changed epoch restarts the host reader.

**Its heartbeat must never be added to `FARM_REAPER_COMPONENTS`.** `farm.reaper_arm` *adds* a named component's downtime to every live lease's deadline. Letting a watchdog outage move lease clocks would fuse the health plane into lease liveness — the exact fusion this system exists to prevent (`watchdog.go:80-87`).

Stopping the watchdog freezes health at its last observed value. Nothing is marked missing, no lease is touched: a watchdog outage costs nobody a device. The symmetric hazard is real and stated in the recovery ladder's own comment (`ladder.go:500-502`) — with no watchdog running there is no confirmation and the ladder stalls; a stalled ladder leaves broken devices broken, but a ladder driven by a *dead* health plane power-cycles a working rack.
bullets: A device the ADB server can see whose devpath matches no occupied slot is counted and logged at DEBUG (`watchdog.go:530-544`). That is a provisioning gap, not a health problem, and enrolling it is somebody else's job.

Writes are skipped when the state has not changed, using a per-devpath cache — but the database remains the truth: a write that touches zero rows clears the cache entry, and the resync clears the whole cache.
`last_seen_at` is refreshed for every present device in one statement (`touch`, `watchdog.go:755`), separate from health transitions. Freshness is a fact, not a verdict.
A failed write drops that devpath's cache entry so the next snapshot retries, rather than the loop believing a write that never landed.

SELECT component, beat_at, now() - beat_at AS age
  FROM farm.component_heartbeat ORDER BY component;

The per-host key is composed by the binary (cmd/farmd/roles.go:235, :258); internal/watchdog's own DefaultComponent is the bare string "watchdog". Note what is absent: no `enroll` and no `node` row, because those roles are not running here.

sections.heading: The ADB host protocol, spoken natively
sections.body:
`internal/adbwire` is a client for the ADB **server** host protocol, over TCP. It never shells out to the `adb` binary, and the reasons are operational rather than aesthetic.

Shelling out means: no typed errors, so "the server refused this verb" and "the socket died" arrive as the same non-zero exit and get treated the same; no way to bound a single call independently of a process; a subprocess per probe across forty devices on a host; output mangled by whatever the local client version prints; and — the one that matters — no way to guarantee that a target string is a devpath rather than a serial, because you are handing text to somebody else's argument parser.

The framing is small: a 4-hex-digit length prefix followed by the service string, and a reply of `OKAY` or `FAIL` plus a length-prefixed message.

Addressing is `host-usb:<devpath>:<cmd>` (default) or `host-serial:<devpath>:<cmd>`. Both carry a devpath and never a serial; they differ only in which of the server's two parsers resolves it, and server builds differ in which one routes devpath matching, so the choice is configuration rather than semantics.
bullets: A `Client` holds no connection. Every call opens its own, because the host protocol closes a connection after a single host service and because a shared socket would let one slow device stall every health probe on the host.

**Control verbs** (`reconnect`, `reconnect-offline`, `detach`, `attach`) are position-addressed. A `*ProtocolError` means the server refused — an older server may not implement the verb, which is a refusal, not a fault — and a `*TransportError` means the socket failed. A recovery ladder needs that distinction: refusal means "try the next rung", transport failure means "the host itself is unreachable and no rung will help".

The listing parser walks the tail **backwards** over tokens it recognises, because the state field is not one token: a host missing its udev rules reports a whole sentence with spaces and a URL. Splitting on whitespace and taking field 1 mislabels exactly the devices an operator most needs to see.

`(no serial number)` is three whitespace-separated words in a whitespace-separated format. Naively taking field 0 records `(no` as a serial and shifts every later column by two. The parser special-cases it and stores an **empty** serial — which also keeps that device out of `AmbiguousSerials`, where a shared literal would manufacture a collision between every unauthorized device on the host.

An unmodelled `key:value` cannot stop the backwards walk, because the devpath sits to the left of the tail: a server that added a field between them would otherwise leave `Devpath` empty and make the device unaddressable for as long as the field existed.
`host:host-features` is exposed; the bare `host:features` deliberately is not, because it resolves to whichever single device the server feels like picking.

Shell uses `shell,v2,raw:` — v2 multiplexes stdout and stderr and carries a real exit status; `raw` suppresses the pty so output is not mangled by line-ending translation. `ShellResult.Exited` distinguishes "exited 0" from "never told us"; `Truncated` records that the output cap was hit, which does not fail, because a chatty command should not look like a broken device.
`MaxShellPacket` (1 MiB) bounds one frame. The length field is a uint32, so a desynchronised stream would otherwise ask for four gigabytes on the strength of four garbage bytes.

The tracker reconnects with **jittered** backoff. Every host in the farm runs one reader, and an adb server restart hits all of them at once; without jitter they would reconnect in lockstep and keep doing so. Its snapshot channel has depth one with the stale entry dropped, because every snapshot is complete state and the newest strictly supersedes an untaken one — blocking would let a slow consumer stall the socket and turn a bookkeeping delay into an apparent host outage.

sections.heading: The sync protocol: file transfer, natively
sections.body:
`sync:` is an ordinary device-side service — started on a transport exactly like `shell,v2,raw:` — but everything after the `OKAY` that answers it speaks a **different framing**. There is no 4-hex-digit length prefix at all: a message is a 4-byte ASCII id followed by a little-endian uint32, and for the id/length forms, that many bytes of payload.

Nothing in `sync.go` may touch `conn.writeMessage`, `conn.readMessage` or `conn.readStatus`. Mixing the two framings is the classic way to desynchronise this stream, and a desynchronised stream does not fail loudly: it reads four arbitrary bytes as a length and asks for that many.

Three properties are load-bearing.

**Transfers stream.** One fixed staging buffer of `SyncDataMax` (64 KiB) carries every chunk in both directions, so a 200 MB artifact costs 64 KiB of heap and not 200 MB — which across twenty-eight devices in one process is the difference between 1.8 MB and 5.6 GB.

**A length from the far end is checked before it is used, and never used to size anything.** A peer that says a DATA chunk is 0xFFFFFFFF bytes is not asking for four gigabytes of memory; it is failing to speak the protocol, and the session is marked broken.

**Every transfer is bounded by the context it was handed, not the context the session was opened with.** A session lasts as long as the work using it; one transfer lasts as long as the budget somebody wrote down for that step. A device that stops answering *without closing anything* — no error, no EOF, no reset — is exactly where those diverge, and a transfer bounded only by its session would hold a step open for the whole of the work's remaining time. When the caller's deadline is what ends a transfer, the result is a `*CanceledError` — a caller getting what it asked for — never a `*TransportError` blaming the wire.
bullets: Requests are strictly sequential: the protocol has no request ids, so two interleaved transfers on one session would read each other's replies. That is not left to a caller to remember — a second request while one is in flight is refused as a `UsageError`.

`Close` is safe from another goroutine at any time; it is how a blocked transfer is interrupted. Its courtesy `QUIT` is **skipped** while a transfer is in flight, because eight bytes landing in the middle of a DATA chunk would corrupt the file being written. It also has a fixed 2s bound rather than a caller's context, because `Close` is deferred on paths that have no context left and must return.

`Push` checks the context **every chunk**, not just at the socket: a cancelled push stops at the next chunk boundary instead of running a multi-gigabyte artifact to completion for a caller that stopped caring, and a source that keeps answering `(0, nil)` — legal for an `io.Reader`, and the shape a wedged pipe takes — cannot spin forever without touching the socket the deadline lives on.
The chunk header is written from the same buffer as the payload, so one chunk is one write. Two writes per chunk would put a 4-byte segment in front of every 64 KiB of a multi-gigabyte transfer.

`Pull` checks for a short write even when `Write` returns nil. The destination is caller-supplied — in the runner it feeds a content-addressed store — and a writer that quietly consumed less than it was given would put one file on the wire, a different file in the store, and a valid digest of the wrong bytes on the step row. Nothing downstream could tell.

A source that dies mid-push is reported as itself, not dressed up as a transport failure or a refusal. The device is fine and the socket is fine; the session is finished either way, because the daemon is mid-file and will never be told how the file ends.

`SEND` joins path and mode with a comma and the daemon splits on the **last** one, so a remote path containing commas is legal and needs no escaping. The mode goes out in **decimal**: the daemon parses it with a base-detecting conversion, so `0755` would be read as octal while `493` is read as decimal — the same number.

POSIX `st_mode` bits are translated explicitly, not conflated with Go's `fs.FileMode` (which is its own encoding, and conflating the two silently turns a directory into a file with peculiar permissions).

`LSTAT_V1` has **no FAIL for a missing path** — the daemon answers a failed lstat with a zeroed reply. `FileInfo.Exists` is inferred from a mode of zero and from nothing else, which is what makes `Stat` usable as an existence check.
`FileInfo.Size` comes from a uint32, so a file of 4 GiB or more is reported modulo 2^32. A caller that must be exact about such a file should read it rather than stat it.

gaps.what: The hardware-fingerprint rung of farm.resolve_device cannot execute on PostgreSQL 17. It calls `min(d.id)` on a uuid column (migrations/00004_operate.sql:284), and this server has no `min(uuid)` aggregate. The project's docker-compose.yml:33 pins `postgres:17-alpine` and nothing anywhere declares a version requirement.
gaps.consequence: Any resolution that reaches rung 2 with a non-NULL fingerprint raises SQLSTATE 42883, "function min(uuid) does not exist". A brand-new phone — no brand, readable properties, therefore a computed fingerprint — hits rung 2 on its very first sighting and NEVER reaches rung 3 or adoption. enroll.classifyResolveError maps 42883 to resolution `pending` (enroll.go:800-806), so the sighting is recorded forever as pending and the device never joins the fleet. That handler even logs "check the PostgreSQL version against migrations/00004_operate.sql", so the failure was anticipated but never documented or gated. Verified live: `SELECT to_regprocedure('min(uuid)')` returns NULL on PostgreSQL 17.10 while `min(bigint)` resolves, and calling resolve_device with a fingerprint raises 42883 at function line 30. Until this is fixed, brand devices out of band before enrolling them, or run a server that has the aggregate.

gaps.what: farm.resolve_device can never RETURN 'ambiguous' from the serial rung. Rung 3 assigns `v_res := 'ambiguous'` on a duplicated serial (00004_operate.sql:306) but leaves `v_dev` NULL, and rung 4 tests only `IF v_dev IS NULL` (:313), so it falls straight through to adoption and overwrites the verdict with 'adopted_new'.
gaps.consequence: An unbranded, un-fingerprinted phone carrying a clone serial in an empty slot is adopted as a NEW device instead of being flagged for a human — verified live in a rolled-back transaction, a third row appeared carrying 0123456789ABCDEF. If the slot is already occupied the adoption fails on devices_one_per_slot (23505) and the enroller records `conflict` instead. Either way the operator never sees `ambiguous` from a serial collision. Only a fingerprint collision (rung 2) can produce it, and rung 2 is itself unreachable on PostgreSQL 17.

gaps.what: Neither topology discovery nor enrollment runs anywhere except the `farmd node` role, and topo.Sysfs refuses to run off Linux (sysfs.go:211-215).
gaps.consequence: The live demo (cmd/farmd/roles.go:311-362) starts demo, api, scheduler, reaper, recovery, jobrunner and per-host watchdogs — not enroll, not topo. farm.identity_observations and farm.slot_occupancy are both EMPTY on the running system (verified: 0 rows each), all 56 devices have hw_fingerprint IS NULL, and farm.component_heartbeat has no `enroll` or `node` row. Everything in the enrollment and topology sections above was verified by calling the SQL functions directly, by running the Go functions in isolation, and by reading the code; the loops themselves have never run here. Nothing in this repository can enroll a device or register a slot on a Windows or macOS host.

gaps.what: Only internal/adbwire's Prometheus collectors are ever registered. internal/api/server.go:355-374 registers obs.Register(...) and adbwire.Collectors() and nothing else; watchdog.Collectors() (watchdog.go:973), topo.Collectors() (discover.go:1098), enroll.Collectors() (enroll.go:1201), recovery's Collectors() (ladder.go:1445), scheduler's, reaper's, jobrunner's and node's have no callers at all.
gaps.consequence: Every metric those packages define is dead code. farm_watchdog_flap_damped_total, farm_watchdog_ambiguous_serials, farm_watchdog_devices_unmapped, farm_watchdog_health_transitions_total, farm_topo_slots_registered_total / slots_retired_total / power_domain_corrections_total / last_success_timestamp_seconds, farm_enroll_cycles_total and farm_recovery_refusals_total cannot be scraped. Verified: GET /metrics exposes 17 metric families and none of them are in those namespaces. An alert written against any of those names will never fire, including one meant to page when discovery stops succeeding. What IS exposed for this area: farm_device_health{state,host,hub}, farm_adb_transport_blips_total, farm_recovery_attempts_total (from internal/obs, not from the ladder), farm_slot_rearm_pending.

gaps.what: internal/enroll, internal/topo and internal/watchdog have zero test files. Of twenty internal packages only internal/adbwire (4 test files) and internal/jobspec (2) are tested.
gaps.consequence: The identity ladder's Go side, the USB tree parser, the mass-removal guard, the rack-label collision checks and the flap damper are all unexercised by `go test ./...` — verified: the three packages report "no test files". The two SQL defects above would each have been caught by one test. Treat behaviour in these packages as documented-but-unverified unless you have watched it run.

gaps.what: The node agent wires Enroll to enroll.EnrollOnce (cmd/farmd/roles.go:495-498), which runs one pass and returns, but node.Agent.enrollLoop (internal/node/agent.go:735-776) expects a function that runs until its context ends and treats every return as an abnormal restart.
gaps.consequence: In the shipped `farmd node` wiring, every enrollment cycle logs WARN "enrollment returned without an error before the agent was asked to stop; restarting it", then backs off 2s, 4s, 8s, 16s, 30s (DefaultEnrollBackoff=2s, DefaultEnrollBackoffMax=30s). Because enrollHealthyRun is a minute and a pass finishes in far less, the backoff never resets: the effective interval settles at 30s — close to enroll.DefaultInterval by accident — but every single cycle emits a warning that reads like a fault, which trains operators to ignore the one log line that would tell them enrollment really broke. enroll.Enroller.Run (enroll.go:241) and topo.Discoverer.Run (discover.go:431) have no callers, so Config.Interval is dead in both packages.

gaps.what: topo.Config's Overrides, RetireVanished, IncludeRootHubs, AdoptEmpty, MinPorts, DryRun and MaxRetireFraction are not wired to any config field or flag. cmd/farmd/roles.go:458-464 constructs it with Pool, HostID, Source, Actor and Logger only.
gaps.consequence: Removal reconciliation is OFF in every shipped deployment: a hub you unplug leaves its slots `active` forever, and they simply never have a device in them. There is no supported way to supply a HubTokens or SlotLabels override map — the label an operator reads in the rack cannot be corrected without editing Go and rebuilding, and on a host with more than one hub per bus the derived labels are dotted (H3.1, H3.2) rather than the H1..H4 the demo shows. There is also no dry-run surface for checking what a first discovery pass would create before it writes.

gaps.what: There is no operator surface for registering a slot, re-slotting a device, or rebranding one. The API's physical endpoints are GET /api/v1/topology, POST /api/v1/slots/{id}/power, POST /api/v1/devices/{id}/exec and POST /api/v1/hosts/{id}/drain|undrain (internal/api/router.go:73-82). farm.register_slot is SQL-only; enroll.Brander.Rebrand (brand.go:264) has no callers anywhere; adbwire.Client.UnsafeBySerial has none outside its test.
gaps.consequence: Bootstrapping a rack on a host that cannot run discovery, or correcting a device whose row is provably wrong, means hand-written SQL against farm.register_slot and farm.devices. The brand-conflict error tells the operator "one of those two device rows is wrong and a human must retire it" (brand.go:127-129) and gives them no command with which to do it.

gaps.what: The SQL role firewall is defined but not assumed at runtime. openPool (cmd/farmd/roles.go:54-75) connects with whatever DATABASE_URL says, and no Go process issues SET ROLE. The only SET ROLE in the system is inside farm.lease_reclaim (migrations/00002_lease.sql:533), which strips the reaper's device_runtime privilege for that function's duration.
gaps.consequence: `REVOKE ALL ON farm.leases FROM farm_watchdog` binds only if you give each role its own login role and DSN — and you cannot today without extra DDL, because farm_reaper, farm_scheduler and farm_watchdog are all created NOLOGIN (verified: rolcanlogin = f for all three). The live demo connects as `farm`, which is a superuser (rolsuper = t), so the watchdog process there could write a lease if its code tried to. The protection actually in force is the Go import barrier, which is real but is a compile-time property of this build, not a database guarantee.
